sections.title: 1. Definition & Overview: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO)
sections.content: Herpes Zoster Ophthalmicus (HZO) is a viral disease caused by the reactivation of the Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) in the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V). It is characterized by a unilateral vesicular rash typically respecting the midline, affecting the forehead, scalp, and nose, accompanied by significant ocular involvement in 50-70% of cases. Early and adequate antiviral therapy is crucial to mitigate disease severity and prevent long-term complications.

references.citation: 177 Comparison of two acyclovir tablet formulations for acute herpes zoster treatment. Antiviral Research. 1993

branches: Primary Infection (Chickenpox) → VZV establishes latent infection in sensory ganglia (trigeminal, dorsal root).
Reactivation Factors: Immunosuppression (age, disease, drugs), trauma, stress.
Viral Replication: Reactivated VZV multiplies, travels anterograde along sensory nerves.
Dermatomal Manifestation: Reaches skin, causing characteristic vesicular rash in affected dermatome (V1 for HZO).
Ocular Involvement: VZV spreads to ocular tissues via direct neural pathways or viremia, causing inflammation & damage.

sections.title: 4. Clinical Features & Symptoms: The HZO Spectrum
content: Prodromal Phase (2-4 days): Fever, malaise, headache, burning, itching, or tingling in the affected dermatome (V1).

Acute Eruptive Phase: Erythematous maculopapular rash, rapidly progressing to vesicles/bullae, pustules, then crusts. Typically unilateral, respecting midline. Distribution along forehead, upper eyelid, nose (Hutchinson's sign).
Pain: Severe, neuropathic, often disproportionate to rash.
Ocular Symptoms: Redness, pain, photophobia, blurred vision, discharge, foreign body sensation.

sections.title: 5. Ocular Examination Findings: A Comprehensive Look

rows: Vesicular rash, edema, ptosis, cicatricial changes
Follicular/papillary conjunctivitis, episcleritis, scleritis (often nodular & necrotizing)
Punctate epithelial keratitis, pseudodendrites (VZV dendrites), stromal keratitis (disciform, neurotrophic), limbal vasculitis, corneal ulceration/perforation
Anterior uveitis (granulomatous/non-granulomatous, KP, synechiae), secondary glaucoma, sectoral iris atrophy
Acute retinal necrosis (ARN), progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN) - rare, severe
Ophthalmoplegia (CN III, IV, VI palsies) - usually transient
Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (PHN) - debilitating neuropathic pain >3 months after rash resolution

sections.title: 6. Investigations & Diagnostic Workup
content: Clinical Diagnosis: Often sufficient based on characteristic rash and V1 involvement.
Viral PCR: Gold standard for atypical cases. Swabs from vesicles, conjunctival/corneal scraping, aqueous/vitreous tap for VZV DNA.
Tzanck Smear: Multinucleated giant cells and intranuclear inclusions (non-specific, distinguishes viral from bacterial/fungal).
Immunofluorescence: Detect VZV antigens in scrapings.
Serology: VZV-specific IgM (acute infection), IgG (immunity/past exposure) - less useful for acute diagnosis.
Imaging: Anterior Segment OCT for corneal changes, B-scan USG for posterior segment inflammation if media opacities preclude fundoscopy.

Localized papules/vesicles, often grouped, pruritic, no dermatomal pattern.

sections.title: 8. Management & Treatment: The Acyclovir Mandate
content: Step 1: Systemic Antiviral Therapy (START WITHIN 72 HOURS OF RASH ONSET)
• Acyclovir (oral): 800 mg PO 5 times daily (q4h while awake) for 7-10 days. Best initiated within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce ocular complications & PHN.
• Valacyclovir (oral): 1000 mg PO TID for 7 days (prodrug of acyclovir, better bioavailability).
• Famciclovir (oral): 500 mg PO TID for 7 days (prodrug of penciclovir, similar efficacy).
Step 2: Topical Ocular Therapy (Based on specific involvement)

• VZV Keratitis: Topical corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1%) for stromal keratitis, combined with prophylactic topical antivirals (Ganciclovir gel 0.15% BID/TID or Acyclovir 3% ointment 5x/day) to prevent HSV superinfection if steroids used. Acyclovir ointment is generally not primary for VZV keratitis but can be used.
• Anterior Uveitis: Topical corticosteroids (e.g., Prednisolone acetate 1% QID), cycloplegics (e.g., Cyclopentolate 1% or Atropine 1% BID-TID).
• Glaucoma: Aqueous suppressants (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists, CAIs).
Step 3: Pain Management
• NSAIDs (oral), Acetaminophen.
• Neuropathic pain: Gabapentin, Pregabalin, TCAs (Amitriptyline), Topical Capsaicin/Lidocaine patches for PHN.
Step 4: Skin Care
• Keep lesions clean and dry, use cool compresses.
• Antibiotics for secondary bacterial infection (rare).

sections.title: 9. Acyclovir: Mechanism of Action – A Viral Assassin
content: Prodrug: Acyclovir is a guanosine analog.
Viral Activation: Selectively phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase (TK) of VZV (and HSV) into acyclovir monophosphate. Host cells lack sufficient TK for this first step.
Host Kinase Phosphorylation: Further phosphorylated by host cellular kinases to acyclovir triphosphate.
DNA Polymerase Inhibition: Acyclovir triphosphate competes with deoxyguanosine triphosphate (dGTP) for incorporation into nascent viral DNA by viral DNA polymerase.
Chain Termination: Once incorporated, acyclovir triphosphate acts as a DNA chain terminator due to the absence of a 3'-hydroxyl group, preventing further elongation.
Result: Irreversible inactivation of viral DNA polymerase, halting viral replication.

rows: Widely distributed into tissues and body fluids, including CSF, aqueous humor, and breast milk.
Minimal hepatic metabolism, primarily excreted unchanged in urine.
Renal (glomerular filtration and tubular secretion); dose adjustment needed in renal failure.

sections.title: 11. Acyclovir Dosing for Acute HZO Treatment
content: Oral: 800 mg PO five times daily (e.g., q4h while awake for 7-10 days).
Intravenous (for severe disease, immunocompromised, or GI malabsorption): 10-15 mg/kg IV every 8 hours for 7-10 days. Requires slower infusion over 1 hour to prevent renal tubular precipitation.
Pediatric Dosing (HZO is rare): 20 mg/kg PO QID (max 800 mg/dose) for 5-7 days.
Renal Impairment: Dose adjustment is critical. E.g., CrCl 25-50 mL/min: 800 mg TID; CrCl 10-25 mL/min: 800 mg BID; CrCl <10 mL/min or hemodialysis: 800 mg QD (post-dialysis).

sections.title: 12. Acyclovir: Prophylaxis in HZO
content: Primary Prevention: The Zoster vaccine (recombinant zoster vaccine, Shingrix®) is recommended for adults ≥50 years (2 doses, 2-6 months apart) and for immunocompromised adults ≥18 years. It is NOT Acyclovir.
Secondary Prophylaxis (Acyclovir):

• Recurrent HZO: Long-term oral acyclovir (e.g., 400 mg BID or 800 mg BID) may be considered, particularly for frequent recurrences or severe disease, similar to HSV prophylaxis. Duration is individualized, often months to years.

• Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (PHN) Prevention: Acute acyclovir treatment reduces PHN incidence and severity. However, there's no strong evidence for long-term acyclovir *after* acute HZO to prevent PHN, unlike its role in treating established PHN.
• Immunocompromised patients: Patients on chronic immunosuppression may require higher prophylactic doses or longer durations, but this is typically for systemic VZV rather than just HZO recurrence.

sections.title: 14. Complications & Prognosis
content: Ocular: Chronic keratitis (neurotrophic, stromal, limbal vasculitis), corneal scarring/perforation, persistent uveitis, secondary glaucoma, cataract, retinal necrosis, optic neuropathy, ophthalmoplegia.
Neurological: Post-Herpetic Neuralgia (PHN) is the most common and debilitating. Other: Zoster sine herpete (pain without rash), contralateral hemiplegia, meningoencephalitis.
Cutaneous: Scarring, hypo/hyperpigmentation, rarely secondary bacterial infection.
Prognosis: Generally good with early antiviral treatment. PHN can persist for months to years, significantly impacting quality of life. Severe ocular complications can lead to permanent vision loss.

sections.title: 15. Red Flags / Emergency Signs in HZO
content: Sudden vision loss or decrease (suggests optic neuritis, ARN, or severe keratitis)
Severe ocular pain unresponsive to standard analgesia
Rapidly worsening corneal ulceration/stromal melt
Signs of acute retinal necrosis (retinal whitening, vasculitis)
New onset diplopia or ophthalmoplegia
Evidence of CNS involvement (e.g., severe headache, altered mental status, focal neurological deficits)
Immunocompromised patient with HZO (higher risk of severe/disseminated disease)

Remembering key ocular manifestations:

E - Episcleritis / Scleritis (often necrotizing)
A - Anterior Uveitis (iritis, trabeculitis, secondary glaucoma)
M - Muscle Palsies (CN III, IV, VI, transient)

sections.title: 17. Key Clinical Pearls for HZO & Acyclovir
content: Hutchinson's Sign (nasociliary nerve involvement, vesicles on tip/side of nose) correlates with a high risk (~75%) of ocular involvement, but its absence does NOT rule out ocular disease.
Start systemic antivirals (Acyclovir, Valacyclovir, Famciclovir) within 72 hours of rash onset for optimal outcomes, especially for PHN prevention.
Even after 72 hours, consider antivirals if new lesions are appearing, if the patient is immunocompromised, or has established ocular involvement.
Always check corneal sensation in HZO patients, as neurotrophic keratitis is a common and serious complication.
Oral steroids are controversial for PHN prevention; generally not recommended acutely unless severe systemic inflammation or optic neuritis, always with concomitant antivirals.
Monitor IOP closely due to risk of trabeculitis and secondary glaucoma.

sections.title: 18. Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Zoster Vaccine (Shingrix®): Recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) approved in 2017/2021, showing >90% efficacy against HZ and PHN, surpassing the live attenuated Zostavax®. This is the most significant advance in HZ prevention.
Extended Release Gabapentin (Gralise®): Newer formulations aiming for improved compliance and reduced side effects for PHN management.
Topical Antivirals for HZO: While systemic antivirals are primary, ongoing research explores novel topical antiviral agents or drug delivery systems for specific ocular manifestations.
Understanding Immunopathogenesis: Deeper insights into host immune response to VZV and mechanisms of viral latency and reactivation are guiding development of targeted therapies.
Pain Management: Focus on multidisciplinary approaches, including nerve blocks and neuromodulation techniques, for refractory PHN.

sections.title: 19. Pediatric / Special Population Considerations
content: Pediatric HZO: Rare in children; usually occurs in those with congenital VZV or early childhood chickenpox. Antiviral dosing is weight-based. Prognosis generally better than in adults, but can be severe in immunocompromised children.

Immunocompromised Patients: HIV/AIDS, transplant recipients, chemotherapy patients. Higher risk of severe, disseminated HZO and complications (e.g., ARN, visceral involvement). IV acyclovir often preferred. Prophylaxis with acyclovir may be indicated for prolonged immunosuppression.

Pregnancy: HZO during pregnancy is rare. Acyclovir is Category B and generally considered safe, especially in severe disease or with significant ocular involvement. Consult with infectious disease and maternal-fetal medicine specialists.
Renal Impairment: Crucial to adjust acyclovir dosage based on creatinine clearance to prevent neurotoxicity (tremors, lethargy, seizures) and renal tubular crystal formation.
